analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent limits on owners prepaying federally assisted low-income housing mortgages and funds nonprofits to buy at-risk affordable housing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its single 1990 referral to two House committees and a subcommittee, it died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1980s, privately owned apartment buildings built with federal help for low-income renters were reaching the point where owners could pay off their federal mortgages early, walk away from the affordability rules, and charge market rents. This bill would make the existing limits on that early payoff permanent, authorize $300 million in grants so public agencies and nonprofits could buy at-risk buildings and keep them affordable for their remaining useful life, and give sellers of such housing a tax break on the sale if they extended the affordability restrictions permanently.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income renters living in federally assisted housing, who would keep affordable homes that might otherwise convert to market rents. Nonprofit organizations and public housing agencies would also gain a funding path ($300 million authorized) to acquire and preserve these buildings, and sellers who voluntarily extend affordability restrictions would pay no tax on the sale gain.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset so the limits on prepaying low-income housing mortgages never expire, keeping privately owned assisted housing affordable to very low-, lower-, and moderate-income families [S3].

Authorizes $300 million in HUD grants to public agencies and nonprofits to acquire eligible low-income housing and retain it as affordable for the property's remaining useful life, with preference for groups serving the poorest tenants for the longest terms [S3].

Excludes from federal income tax any gain on the sale of qualified low-income housing sold under a HUD-approved plan that permanently extends the affordability restrictions, giving owners a financial reason to sell to preservers instead of converting to market rents [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of federally assisted multifamily housing, who would permanently lose the option to prepay their federal mortgages, exit the affordability restrictions, and re-let units at market rates. Federal taxpayers would fund the $300 million grant program and forgo tax revenue on excluded sale gains.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $300 million in spending and a new tax exclusion without any identified offset, adding to federal costs rather than paying for itself [S3].

Making the prepayment limitation permanent binds property owners indefinitely; owners argued they should eventually regain the right to refinance or exit arrangements made decades earlier, and a permanent restriction could discourage investment in the aging assisted-housing stock.

The tax exclusion rewards sellers who were already positioned to negotiate HUD-approved sales, and its benefit flows through a voluntary process that owners could simply decline to use, limiting how much preservation it actually buys.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted: a federal investment that keeps existing affordable apartments from converting to market rents costs far less than building replacements, and the tax exclusion gives owners a path to sell rather than convert. The costs are modest relative to the housing at stake, though the permanent prepayment restriction imposed on owners without compensation is a genuine burden, and the bill's voluntary tax incentive would only reach owners willing to deal. On balance, for the low-income tenants at risk of displacement, the trade favors them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and to a housing subcommittee a week later, and with no markup or floor action ever scheduled, it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Sidney Yates introduced the Low-Income Housing Preservation Act of 1990 in the House on January 23, 1990 [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs and to the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
On February 1, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Development, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, killing the bill [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of federally assisted low-income housing are better off, because the option to prepay their federal mortgages and convert apartments to market rents was never made permanent. The preservation grants and tax incentive died with the bill, so no new federal money went to nonprofit and public buyers of at-risk housing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of assisted housing, not tenants

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill attracted only three sponsors before it died in committee [S4].

industries.industry: Owners of federally assisted multifamily housing
industries.note: These owners prepay federal mortgages once permitted, exit affordability restrictions, and re-rent at market rates, which is exactly what the bill would permanently block. Their financial gain comes directly out of low-income tenants' housing security.

industries.industry: Nonprofit housing organizations and public housing agencies
industries.note: The bill authorizes $300 million in HUD grants for them to acquire at-risk buildings and keep them affordable for the properties' remaining useful life, so their gain and tenants' benefit point the same direction.

industries.industry: Real estate investors and sellers of assisted housing
industries.note: Sellers who extend affordability restrictions under a HUD-approved plan would pay no tax on the sale gain, a real benefit, but the permanent prepayment ban limits their long-term exit options.
